Define an $a \times b$ cell loop in a $2n \times 2n$ grid of cells to be the $2a + 2b - 4$ cells that surround an $(a - 2) \times (b - 2)$ (possibly empty) rectangle of cells in the grid. For example, the following diagram shows a way to partition a $6 \times 6$ grid of cells into $4$ cell loops.

| P   P P   P | Y   Y |
| P | R R | P | Y | Y |
| P | R R | P | Y | Y |
| P   P P   P | Y | Y |
| G   G G   G | Y | Y |
| G   G G   G | Y   Y |

Find the number of ways to partition a $10 \times 10$ grid of cells into $5$ cell loops so that every cell of the grid belongs to exactly one cell loop.

## **1. Understanding the definition**

A "cell loop" is defined as: the \( 2a + 2b - 4 \) cells that surround an \((a-2) \times (b-2)\) rectangle of cells.

- The "surrounding cells" are like a rectangular **border** of thickness 1.  
- If \(a\) = height, \(b\) = width, the border has \(a\) rows and \(b\) columns, but only the cells in the outer boundary (not the inner rectangle) are part of the loop.

Thus, the **loop** is a **rectangular ring** of dimensions \(a \times b\) (grid size), with **area** \(ab - (a-2)(b-2) = ab - (ab - 2a - 2b + 4) = 2a + 2b - 4\).

Constraint: \(2 \le a, b \le 2n\), \(n=5\) here (\(10\times 10\) grid).
